text: Scoring a risk, whether with a quick likelihood times impact guess or a full FAIR analysis, doesn't actually change anything on its own. Every scored risk still needs a treatment decision: what, specifically, is the organization going to do about it? ISO 31000 names four options, and this lesson closes out the chapter by walking through all four, plus the register that makes each decision stick.

Accepting a risk means formally deciding to take no further action, because the cost of fixing it outweighs the benefit, or it already fits the organization's risk appetite. Done right, that's a documented, signed-off decision. A risk that just sits there because nobody got to it isn't acceptance — it's an unmanaged gap, and that distinction matters enormously the moment an auditor asks who approved it.

Mitigation reduces likelihood, impact, or both, through an actual control — hardware-key MFA to cut down successful credential theft, or immutable backups to shrink the blast radius of ransomware. It's most security teams' default instinct, and usually the right one, but it's never free, which is exactly why the quantitative question from two lessons ago, is this worth the spend, matters here.

Transfer shifts who pays for a risk, through cyber-insurance or a contract clause like vendor indemnification — it does not make the underlying exposure disappear. Insurers exclude plenty of scenarios and cap payouts, and an indemnification clause is only worth what the other party can actually pay. Avoidance goes further: it eliminates the activity entirely, not just reduces it, by killing a feature, retiring a legacy system, or exiting a jurisdiction — which is why it usually needs a business decision-maker, since it collides directly with what the business wants to do.

None of these four decisions means anything without a risk register tracking it: the risk, its score, its owner, the treatment chosen, any actions and deadlines, and a review date, because both the risk and the business keep changing. Without that, a treatment decision is just a meeting nobody remembers. With it, risk management stops being a one-time exercise and becomes the ongoing program Chapter 4 picks up next, starting with what a real GRC program actually coordinates.
